transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-24
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood SE); Sara G., Tom A., Priya N., Mike R. (Pine & Oak)

Summary:
Quick interactive demo of Redwood Hosted API for chat/text generation. Focus on streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), retry/backoff patterns and a checklist for an upcoming pilot. Security implications discussed (HIPAA, KMS) and private/dedicated options briefly covered.

Topics:
- Streaming basics and token flushing
- Generation params and cost/latency tradeoffs
- Retry semantics, idempotency and backoff
- Prefix/KV cache and repeated context performance
- Security: encryption, SOC2, HIPAA concerns and private deployment options
- Pilot checklist and next steps

Action items (quick): see metadata list above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, and we'll jump into a short hands-on demo of the hosted chat/text gen end points and then go through a retry/checklist for your pilot.
[00:18] Sara (Pine & Oak - CTO): Thanks Maya. We, um, have a tight timeline, about four weeks to a pilot — security gating is our big blocker.
[00:25] Maya: Totally understood — we'll cover the security docs and KMS notes. Liam, do you want to kick off the console demo?
[00:30] Liam (Redwood SE): Sure. Sharing screen — this is the Redwood Console playground, but everything I'll show is the same via the REST SDK. First, I'll do a small chat gen stream so you can see latency and token streaming behavior.
[00:46] [screen noise, short pause]
[01:05] Liam: Starting a conversation with system instruction + user turn. We set temperature 0.2, max_tokens 120 and enable streaming. You'll see partial tokens come in — this is chunked by the runtime and by default we flush partial frames every 200ms or when punctuation is emitted, that helps keep low latency without burning tokens.
[01:35] Tom (Lead ML Eng): That flush interval — can we tune it? For us, sub-200ms is ideal for chat UI.
[01:42] Liam: Yes, there's a streaming config and client-side buffering. You can set smaller flush windows, but there's a tradeoff: more frequent flushes slightly increase token overhead and network calls. For web UIs we usually recommend 100-200ms.
[02:05] Priya (Security): When you say token overhead — is any extra content logged in the control plane? We need to ensure PHI isn't persisted.
[02:12] Maya: Good question. For hosted accounts we offer configurable retention and opt-out for logging of prompts. We'll share the SOC2 + HIPAA guidance doc. For strict PHI workflows customers typically go Dedicated or Private where logs and keys stay in customer-controlled KMS.
[02:38] Mike (SRE): If we go Private, do you still manage the control plane? What's the boundary?
[02:45] Jordan (Redwood SE): For VPC/Private, control plane is customer-visible and you can run the inference nodes in your VPC. We integrate with your KMS/HSM for key material. We'll send a diagram, but short answer: you own the network and keys, Redwood provides the runtime and orchestration.
[03:05] [05s crosstalk]
[03:12] Liam: Back to retries — typical failure modes are transient resource limits (429s), occasional kernel OOMs on heavy sequences, and network blips. Our SDKs implement an exponential backoff with jitter by default and an idempotency token option for non-fatal duplicate suppression.
[03:33] Tom: Idempotency token — how does that work for streaming responses? If the connection drops mid-stream, can we resume?
[03:40] Liam: Good one. We support resumable streams in the console sandbox and the hosted API via a resume token — it's not a byte-for-byte resume, it's a resume from the last confirmed token index. There's a short lived cache of the last N KV-cache states to allow reasonable resume. If you need stricter resume semantics we recommend a checkpointing pattern on the client to replay the last user prompt plus confirmed response suffix.
[04:05] Sara: How much does that cache cost us? Is it charged per token?
[04:10] Maya: Cache is a runtime optimization, not billed per se — you pay token generation + model compute. We'll include a simple cost breakdown in the pricing doc.
[04:20] [04:20] Liam: Now I'll show parameter impacts — same prompt, set temperature 0.0 vs 0.9 and top_p. Notice deterministic output at low temp; higher temp increases variability and can make hallucinations more likely. For customer-facing assistants we suggest temperature 0.0-0.3 and use top_p like 0.85 for constrained creativity.
[04:55] Tom: For our triage flow we need deterministic summarization — low temp makes sense. What about max_tokens and truncation?
[05:03] Liam: You can set max_tokens per response; we also support stop sequences and structured outputs (JSON schema enforcement). For truncation, we recommend prefix KV caching so repeated context (like instructions and user profile) doesn't re-tokenize every time. That reduces latency and cost.
[05:30] Priya: Are there hooks for audit logs and per-request metadata? We need to tie events back to user sessions in our logs.
[05:36] Maya: Yes, per-request metadata and request IDs are surfaced in the console, and you can export logs to your SIEM. For private deployments we can push audit logs directly to your cloud storage.
[05:48] [06:00] 
[06:10] Liam: Demo: show a 500-user concurrency test in the sandbox — we'll simulate multiple parallel chat clients and watch queueing and batching.
[06:22] [simulation noise]
[06:48] Liam: You see the throughput rise; our continuous batching groups small requests to maximize GPU utilization while respecting latency SLOs. If a request is latency-sensitive you can set a policy to route to a low-latency pool (smaller batch, higher cost). That's a common pattern.
[07:10] Tom: Can we set per-route SLOs? Like route /triage to low-latency and /bulk to high-throughput?
[07:16] Jordan: Yep — routing policies per API key or route, with automatic fallback to cheaper model variants if capacity issues arise. We'll include a sample routing policy YAML.
[07:30] Sara: About model variants — do you auto-quantize?
[07:34] Liam: We ship curated variants and have quantization profiles. For sensitive workloads we recommend evaluating accuracy impact before switching; Optimize suggests profiles based on evals you run.
[07:50] [08:00] 
[08:05] Tom: Ok, practical: what's in the pilot checklist? We need a minimal list to unblock us.
[08:10] Maya: Good — our recommended pilot checklist: 1) Identify sample prompts and test dataset with redaction; 2) run a small benchmark (we'll provide script); 3) confirm network routing and VPC requirements; 4) review security docs + KMS options; 5) agree on success metrics (latency p95 < 250ms, cost per 1k tokens target).
[08:35] Priya: Success metric — we also need to confirm data retention policy and encryption at rest for the pilot.
[08:40] Maya: We'll include explicit retention toggles and KMS integration steps in the security pack.
[08:48] [09:00] 
[09:15] Liam: Quick note on retries: best practice is optimistic retry for idempotent calls — e.g., send an idempotency_key and retry up to 3 times with exponential backoff 200ms -> 800ms. For in-flight streams, client should request resume, and if resume fails, treat as fresh request with the same idempotency_key to avoid double side effects on downstream systems.
[09:45] Tom: If there are billing implications for duplicate tokens generated during retries, how do you handle that?
[09:51] Liam: We try to make retries cheap: duplicate token generations under 500ms are generally de-duped in the billing engine when possible, but for long replays we advise clients to detect partial responses client-side and reconcile before reissuing heavy requests.
[10:10] Sara: We use an internal eventing system — must guarantee exactly-once semantics for downstream ops, so idempotency is critical.
[10:18] Jordan: For side-effecting operations we recommend designing a separate mutate endpoint that accepts server-checked idempotency keys and uses a write-ahead log in your backend. Keep the model generation purely read-only; then you can gate side effects after you confirm the result.
[10:35] [10:40] 
[10:50] Priya: On encryption: we need envelope encryption with our KMS. Does Redwood support customer-managed keys?
[10:56] Maya: Yes — both Dedicated and Private support CMK integration. Hosted can integrate via a bring-your-own-key flow for enterprise tiers; we'll send the exact steps.
[11:10] Tom: Do you have benchmarks on p95 latency for the 1.3B vs 7B-ish models on common A100 or equivalent?
[11:18] Liam: We do. I'll attach a small benchmark pack but rough numbers: optimized 7B at typical token length 64 runs ~60-120ms p50 and p95 around 180-260ms on a modern A100-ish serving tier with batching tuned. We'll share concrete numbers in the doc for the model you pick.
[11:40] Sara: That's promising. Our UI target is p95 < 250ms, so it seems feasible.
[11:46] [12:00] 
[12:05] Liam: One more demo: show recovering from a simulated 502 mid-stream.
[12:12] [simulation beeps]
[12:30] Liam: Client saw a socket close at token index 42; client called resume with the resume token, server returned last confirmed index 40 and resumed. If resume is not available we fallback to a fresh request with the same idempotency_key and short-circuit duplicate handlers.
[12:50] Tom: Nice — what's the retention window for the resume cache?
[12:54] Liam: Default is 60s ephemeral cache; can be configured on Dedicated/Private to be longer but there's memory tradeoff. We'll document recommended values.
[13:10] [13:20] 
[13:30] Priya: A question on redaction — we can't send raw PHI even in synthetic tests. Do you have client-side redaction helpers?
[13:36] Maya: We have reference redaction libraries and recommend pre-tokenization redaction before sending. For pilot we can accept a hashed placeholder token if you need to test semantics. We'll include sample code.
[13:50] Sara: Traffic shaping — we may spike during peak triage windows, is bursting supported?
[13:56] Jordan: Yes — Dedicated has burst capacity and autoscale options with predictable warm-up. For hosted accounts we offer burst pooling; if you're above a threshold we'd recommend a Dedicated pool or hybrid routing.
[14:20] [14:30] 
[14:40] Mike: Any SLA for streaming latency?
[14:44] Maya: Dedicated customers can get SLA-backed latency SLOs. Hosted has published performance profiles but not strict SLA unless you upgrade. We'll include the SLA matrix.
[15:00] Tom: Ok — for the pilot we'll try hosted first with a small dedicated pool if needed.
[15:07] Maya: That sounds reasonable and is a nice ramp strategy.
[15:12] [15:20] 
[15:25] Liam: Quick pointer on cost controls: per-route token caps, sampling-based caching, and the Optimize recommendations engine which can suggest quantized variants when your eval shows minimal quality drop.
[15:40] Tom: How do we define those evals? Is there an automated harness?
[15:44] Jordan: Optimize has an eval runner you can feed a prompt set into; it outputs score deltas and cost estimates for each model/quantization profile. We'll share a demo notebook.
[16:05] Sara: Please send that notebook.
[16:10] Maya: Will do — links in next steps.
[16:15] [16:30] 
[16:35] Liam: One more operational note: when you do a POC, try to run both the small bench and a synthetic spike. Look for tokenization hotspots — long system prompts can blow up token counts. Our recommendation: keep static instruction as a cached prefix and send dynamic user text separately.
[16:58] Tom: Noted. We'll supply sample prompts and expected distributions.
[17:05] Priya: We need a security review session with our compliance folks — are you available next week?
[17:12] Maya: Yes — I'll coordinate. We'll include our security SME on that call.
[17:20] [17:30] 
[17:40] Sara: Timeline recap — pilot in 4 weeks, security review this week, bench script and dataset ready in two weeks.
[17:48] Maya: Recap and next steps: we'll send pricing + security pack + bench script + routing policy sample and schedule the security review. Anything else?
[17:58] Tom: Please include a minimal code sample for streaming resume in python.
[18:04] Liam: I'll add that to the bench repo.
[18:10] Priya: Make sure KMS steps are explicit.
[18:15] Maya: Will do.
[18:20] [18:30] 
[18:35] Jordan: Quick note — I'll also include a YAML snippet for per-route SLOs so your infra team can eyeball it quickly.
[18:45] Mike: Thanks.
[18:48] Maya: Any final questions?
[18:50] Sara: None from me, thanks.
[18:54] [19:00] 
[19:05] Liam: Links we'll share in the follow-up: deck (https://redwood.ai/decks/chat-onramp.pdf), security pack (https://redwood.ai/security.pdf), bench script repo (https://github.com/redwood-inference/pilot-bench), and an example routing policy gist.
[19:30] Tom: Great.
[19:35] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the items and calendar invites.
[19:40] [Call ends — total 52 min]
